Chapter 8.2

How Can the Number of Protons in an Atom Be Used to Identify an Element?

The one number that tells you which element you are holding

Two elements can look alike, weigh the same and sit side by side. What makes them different substances?

Learning Objectives

What you will be able to do by the end

1Read the proton number of an element from the periodic table.
2Explain why no two elements can have the same number of protons.
3Name an element when you are given the number of protons in its atom.
4Describe how scientists create elements that are not found on Earth.
5Explain why arranging elements by proton number fixed the problems in Mendeleev’s table.

Lesson 1 covers objectives 1 and 2 and ends at the retrieval slide. Lesson 2 covers objectives 3, 4 and 5.

Core concept

What is the proton number?

Every element’s tile carries two numbers. The proton number is the smaller one, and it is the number of protons in one atom of that element.

Learn
  • At present, there are 118 elements that have been discovered, either naturally occurring or created in a laboratory.Some were dug out of the ground. Others have never been found on Earth at all and were built by scientists on purpose.
  • Every tile carries two numbers. The proton number is the smaller of them. The larger number is the relative atomic mass, which for most atoms is close to the protons and neutrons counted together.Most tiles in this chapter print the proton number above the symbol, but many data booklets and wall charts print it below. Do not learn the position — learn that it is the smaller number, and check it against where the element sits in the table.
  • This is the number of protons in an atom of an element. For example, the proton number of helium is 2, which means that a helium atom contains two protons.Read the number, and you know how many protons are packed into the nucleus of every single atom of that element.
  • Elements are arranged in the periodic table in order of increasing number of protons.Start at the top left and walk along the rows. The count goes up by one at every step, with no gaps and no repeats.
Key Facts
  • The proton number is the number of protons in an atom of an element.
  • Elements are arranged in the periodic table in order of increasing number of protons.
  • There are 118 elements discovered so far, either naturally occurring or created in a laboratory.
  • The proton number is the smaller of the two numbers on a tile. Some charts print it above the symbol and some below — check the chart you are reading.

Core concept

Why can no two elements have the same number of protons?

The number of protons is what tells one element apart from another, so it has to be unique.

Learn
  • No two elements can have the same number of protons in their atoms.If two substances had the same count of protons, there would be nothing left to tell them apart. They would be the same element.
  • The number of protons in atoms differentiates one element from another.Change the number of protons and you have changed which element you are holding. Nothing else about an atom does that.
  • Elements are different from one another as they have unique atomic structures.Every element is built to its own recipe, and the count of protons is the first line of that recipe.
  • A hydrogen atom has 1 proton, a helium atom has 2 protons, and a lithium atom has 3 protons.Those are the first three boxes in the table, and they climb by exactly one each time.
  • The number of neutrons can differ between atoms of the same element, so it cannot be used to identify an element.Same protons, different neutrons — still the same element. Two atoms with 6 protons are both carbon whether they carry 6 neutrons or 8.
Key Facts
  • No two elements can have the same number of protons in their atoms.
  • The number of protons differentiates one element from another.
  • The number of neutrons can differ between atoms of the same element, so it cannot be used to identify an element.
  • An atom has no overall charge, so the number of electrons equals the number of protons. That stops being true once an atom gains or loses electrons — but that is next chapter.

Core concept

Why do hydrogen, helium and lithium behave so differently?

Three elements sit next to each other in the table, and one proton apart is enough to change everything about them.

Learn
  • Hydrogen, helium and lithium have different numbers of protons in their atoms.One, two and three. Those three numbers are the whole reason the three substances are not the same.
  • Thus, they have different physical and chemical properties.Physical properties are things you can observe without changing the substance, such as whether it is a solid or a gas. Chemical properties are about what it reacts with.
  • Lithium is a soft solid metal, helium is a gas light enough to lift a balloon, and hydrogen is a gas squeezed into a steel cylinder.Squeezing hydrogen will not turn it into a liquid. To do that you have to cool it to about −253 °C. That is another physical property that belongs to hydrogen and to no other element.
  • The number of protons in an atom of an element therefore decides far more than a place in a table.It sets what the element is, and what it is decides everything else about how it looks and behaves.
Key Facts
  • Elements with different numbers of protons have different physical and chemical properties.
  • Elements are different from one another as they have unique atomic structures.

Think first

If an element has never existed on Earth, how would anyone even know what to look for? And once you have made a single atom of it that lasts a thousandth of a second, how do you prove to the rest of the world that you made it?

Hold on to that second question. You will answer it yourself on the accelerator slide, and then see how the element 113 team did it.

📓Now complete your notes: Section C: How new elements are createdWrite the section title, and write the number 92 next to it.
Core concept

How do scientists create an element that is not found on Earth?

There are no naturally occurring elements with more than 92 protons on Earth, so anything beyond that has to be built.

Learn
  • There are no naturally occurring elements with more than 92 protons on Earth.Uranium, with 92 protons, is where nature stops. Everything past it has to be made. (Chemists have since found the faintest traces of two heavier elements inside uranium ore — but only a few atoms in a whole rock. For this chapter the answer is 92.)
  • Scientists can create elements by colliding atoms of two elements at high speed in a device known as a particle accelerator.Two atoms are thrown at each other hard enough that their nuclei join into one bigger nucleus.
  • The proton numbers of the two elements add up exactly to the proton number of the new element.30 + 83 is always 113. The masses only almost add up, because a neutron or two is usually thrown out at the moment the two nuclei join. For this chapter, add the proton numbers and nothing else.
  • New elements, namely elements 113, 115, 117 and 118, have been discovered by scientists in recent years.The periodic table is not a finished object. Four new boxes have been filled in within living memory.
  • The chance of any one collision making a new atom is about one in a trillion, which is why a team can run a machine for years to make three atoms.A trillion seconds is about thirty-two thousand years. At one collision a second you would have started in the Stone Age.
Key Facts
  • Elements beyond proton number 92 do not occur naturally on Earth and are created in a laboratory.
  • Even when a new element is formed, its atom appears for only about a thousandth of a second before rapidly decaying.
  • The chance of any one collision making a new atom is about one in a trillion.

Worked example

Which element are you making?

Two nuclei join, and their protons all end up in the same nucleus. So the proton numbers add. That is the whole calculation, and you are about to be asked to do it.

Worked for you: zinc fired at bismuth
Read every line. You will do the same three steps in a moment with nothing filled in.
1Write down the proton number of each element.zinc = 30   bismuth = 83
2Add them. The protons of both nuclei end up in one nucleus.30 + 83 = 113
3Look up 113 in the periodic table and read off the name.113 → nihonium
Half done: calcium fired at californium
Two lines are filled in. Say the missing one out loud before you scroll on.
1Write down the proton number of each element.calcium = 20   californium = 98
2Add them.20 + 98 = ?
3Look the answer up in the table.? → ?

20 + 98 = 118, and 118 is oganesson — the last box on the whole chart.

How long does it really take to make one atom?

One collision in an accelerator hardly ever works — but how rarely? Commit to a number before you run the machine, then find out what that number costs in time.

Run the acceleratorlive
1Answer the prediction, then choose two elements, press Run, and watch all four counters at once.
Run the accelerator
Choose a projectile and a target. Their proton numbers add, and that sum decides which element you are trying to build. Then find out how long one atom costs.

Predict first. Roughly how many collisions does a machine need before one atom of a brand new element is made?

30+83=113 protons in the new atom
Making element 113: nihonium

The beam is drawn far slower and far thinner than it runs, so that you can see single nuclei. The counters below run at the full rate you set.

Collisions tried0
Atoms made0
Real time this represents0.0 days
Longest an atom survived–
Atoms made against real time
Try this, and predict before you do: drag the beam rate from 600 up to 3000. You will get your atoms sooner in the lesson, but watch the real time counter at the moment each atom appears. Does the number of real years go down too?
No. The real clock counts collisions, not how fast you watch them. A faster slider only speeds up the lesson, not the physics. To make an atom sooner for real you would need a machine that fires more nuclei every second, which is exactly what the teams building these elements spend their money on.

Honesty box. The real chance of one collision making a new atom is about one in a trillion. Here it is compressed to one in 20 000 so that a success can happen inside a lesson. The clock undoes that compression: it converts your attempts back to the real odds at a real machine rate, calibrated so that four trillion collisions read as nine years, which is what the team that made element 113 actually spent. Expect roughly two to three years of non-stop running per atom; that team ran for nine years and got three atoms. Every atom here is a genuine random draw, so your wait will not match anyone else’s. This model ignores the beam energy, which on a real machine has to be tuned precisely, and it uses nihonium’s decay time (a half-life of about two thousandths of a second) for every element, because the point is the scale, not the exact figure.

Hook

He left an empty box, and told everyone what would be in it

In 1871 Mendeleev had 63 elements and a table with holes in it. Instead of shuffling things along to close a gap, he did something far riskier.

Fifteen years later, in 1886, a German chemist called Winkler found a new element. What do you think happened?

The point of this section

A table you can only read is a list. A table that can tell you about something nobody has found yet is a scientific idea. On the next slide, find out what Mendeleev got wrong — and which number finally fixed it.

📓Now complete your notes: Section D: How the periodic table developedWrite the section title and the year 1871.
History of science

How did the periodic table come to look like this?

The table we use was not designed once and finished. It was corrected, argued over and redrawn more than a thousand times.

Learn
  • Russian chemist Dmitri Ivanovich Mendeleev is widely known as the father of the periodic table.He was the first to arrange the elements into a table that made their pattern obvious.
  • He initially devised a periodic table which included 63 elements that were known to exist. He left gaps in the table to allow for the inclusion of elements that were yet to be discovered.Leaving a gap was a bold move. He was saying that something must exist there, even though nobody had found it yet.
  • His table had some inconsistencies. For example, the element iodine used to be arranged before the element tellurium.Sorted his way, two elements came out in an order that did not fit their properties. That was a sign something was not quite right.
  • Decades later, another scientist discovered that arranging the elements in order of increasing proton numbers could resolve the inconsistencies, which is why tellurium now appears before iodine.Once the elements were ordered by the number of protons instead, the odd cases sorted themselves out.
  • There have been more than a thousand different versions of the periodic table since Mendeleev's first draft, and studies on other ways of classifying elements are still ongoing.The familiar rectangle is only one way of laying the elements out. Spirals, loops and other shapes all show the same pattern differently.
Key Facts
  • Arranging the elements in order of increasing proton number resolved the inconsistencies in Mendeleev's table.
  • The modern version we now use is the product of scientific developments over many years.
Test

Why does tellurium now appear before iodine in the periodic table?
